main_point: The draft is about how the discovery rule should handle software that changes after sale; only in Part III did I learn it proposes starting the clock at the manufacturer's patch note.

look_for.item: The contribution stated against the existing positions the draft names
look_for.quote: This Article explores how the discovery rule applies to software defects and what courts should make of the manufacturer's power to change the product after the sale.
look_for.note: The contribution isn't stated until Part III, and it's never set against the positions described in Part II.B.

look_for.item: Positions the draft argues against, attributed and stated in a form their holders would accept
look_for.quote: In Delacroix v. Omnisync Systems, a Franklin trial court held that a claim involving a defective thermostat update accrued when the plaintiff first noticed the thermostat behaving oddly, even though she had no reason to suspect a software defect.
look_for.note: The judicial positions are attributed and fairly stated.

look_for.item: Claims about the literature ("no scholar has," "the literature ignores") that an expert would test
look_for.quote: No scholar has examined how the discovery rule applies to software defects.
look_for.note: Stated flatly, with one footnote on a different question behind it.

look_for.item: The scope of the claim: what it covers and what it sets aside
look_for.quote: The patch-notice rule applies only where the defect lives in code that the owner cannot see.
look_for.note: Scope is stated, though only at the end of Part III.

look_for.item: Words spent explaining what experts already know, compared with words spent on the new move
look_for.quote: The discovery rule has a long pedigree.
look_for.note: Part I retells the history in eight paragraphs; the proposal gets five.

look_for.item: The obvious objection from within the field, acknowledged
look_for.note: Promised in the roadmap but absent; nothing takes up the manufacturer's control over when disclosure happens.

findings.quote: No scholar has examined how the discovery rule applies to software defects.
findings.issue: A flat novelty claim that experts will test
findings.why_it_matters: Readers in the field tend to read 'no scholar has' as a sign the author hasn't looked, and a single counterexample would undercut the contribution. A precise statement of what's new is safer and more persuasive.

findings.quote: In Pruitt v. Harlan Devices, by contrast, the court held that the claim accrued only when the manufacturer publicly acknowledged the defect.
findings.issue: The draft never says how its rule differs from Pruitt
findings.why_it_matters: As described, Pruitt already ties accrual to the manufacturer's public acknowledgment. An expert will ask what the Article adds beyond picking a side of the split.

findings.quote: This Article explores how the discovery rule applies to software defects and what courts should make of the manufacturer's power to change the product after the sale.
findings.issue: The introduction states a topic, not the claim
findings.why_it_matters: An expert deciding how closely to read wants the proposal and what's new up front; 'explores' signals a survey.

findings.quote: The discovery rule has a long pedigree.
findings.issue: Part I spends most of the draft on history experts know
findings.why_it_matters: Experts will skim it and may miss the one point the argument needs: that the latent-defect cases asked what the manufacturer knew.

findings.quote: Courts should consider the timing of a manufacturer's patch disclosures, among other factors, in deciding when a software claim accrues.
findings.issue: The conclusion is weaker than the proposal in Part III
findings.why_it_matters: An expert will ask which claim the author is defending: a bright-line rule or one factor among many.

what_works.quote: Every version of the discovery rule assumes that the product is fixed at the moment of sale.
what_works.note: The paper's real insight, stated crisply. It belongs in the introduction.

what_works.quote: The lock they bought was not defective. The lock that opened their door was.
what_works.note: Makes the post-sale-change problem concrete in two sentences.

related_work.work: Priya Anand, Is Code a Product?, 61 Franklin L. Rev. 1 (2021)
related_work.why: The draft cites it only on whether software is a product. If it also takes up accrual, the 'no scholar has examined' claim fails, so it's the first thing to reread.

related_work.work: Scholarship on accrual rules and statutes of repose for latent product defects
related_work.why: The closest existing conversation. The draft should say how a disclosure-based trigger differs from the accrual rules that work proposes.
